question: Is currency exchange permissible in Islam, and is Forex trading halal?
answer:
So we begin by stating that the exchange of currencies, in and of themselves, is of course something that is allowed by unanimous consensus and by explicit traditions of the Prophet ﷺ. In the famous hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit reported in Sahih Muslim, our Prophet ﷺ said that exchanging gold for gold, and exchanging silver for silver, and exchanging wheat for wheat, and barley for barley (and in one version salt for salt, and in one version dates for dates), as long as it is done yadan bi-yad. Yadan bi-yad means we do the transaction right then and there: one hand gives, the other hand takes. Sawa'an bi-sawa': it is done with the exact same amount between the two.

So if I give you 10 grams of gold, you need to give me back 10 grams of gold. If I give you 20 grams of silver, you need to give me 20 grams of silver. If I give you one kilo or one pound of dates, you need to give me back one kilo or one pound of dates. So it must be done yadan bi-yad, sawa'an bi-sawa'. Two conditions: spot transaction and the same quantity. Whoever increases or demands an increase has indeed fallen into riba, or interest. I cannot give you $10 and then say, give me back 11. I cannot do that. And also I cannot do less as well. So basically you cannot demand more or less from the amount if it is the same currency or the same item mentioned in this hadith: gold, silver, wheat, barley, dates and salt.

However, then our Prophet said: if you are trading and transacting between these commodities, then go ahead and buy and sell, however the proportions are, as long as it is done as a spot transaction, yadan bi-yad, right then and there. In other words, if I'm going to give you gold and you're going to hand me back barley, obviously I'm not going to give you 10 grams of gold and you're going to give me 10 grams of barley. On the contrary, 10 grams of gold is going to give me many, many, many tons, maybe even, of barley. So the Prophet ﷺ explicitly said: if you are buying and selling between different ones of these commodities, then the exchange rate between them, it is permissible however you decide. But there is one condition that is very explicit, and that is in the hadith in Sahih Muslim: if it is done at the same time frame.

Therefore, currency exchange falls under this hadith, and you are allowed to exchange dollars for pounds. You're allowed to exchange Canadian dollars for American dollars. You're allowed to exchange yen for lira, however you want to do that, with whatever the two parties agree to, and it is up to you. It's not necessary for you to take what is written on a website for the exchange rate. It is up to you and the buyer or the seller, whoever. If they agree to more or less, that's between you and the laws of the land that you live in. I'm not saying if it would be illegal; but I'm saying, if some countries allow it that you don't have to follow the official rates, it is permissible for you to charge more or less, and the other person should know that this is the rate and this is what I'm charging you, and it's up to them if they want to take it or not.

But one condition: the ownership needs to be transferred right then and there. You cannot delay that: "I'm going to give you $100 today, and then you give me back the equivalent in pounds a month from now, whatever that equivalent is." No, it needs to be done right then and there. So if I give you $100, you need to give me back the British pounds right then and there. The transfer of ownership needs to be a spot transaction.

There is no riba if the currencies are different and the amounts are different; only if the currency is the same and the amounts are different. If I give you dollars and you give me back more or less of the same US dollars, then riba will occur. If I give you one currency and you give me a different currency, there is no riba. I hope that is clear.

Now, can this be done with the intention of profit? Yes, why not? There is no haraj, there is no sin, in wanting to make this into a profit. If you feel, for example, that the Japanese yen is going to increase in value in 10 months, whatever, and you say, "You know what? I'm going to store some of my money in the Japanese currency," and so you exchange $10,000 into yen, and then you have it: it is in your hand, or you own it somehow. I mean, it doesn't have to be physical banknotes, but you own it. Ownership, of course, means you have full rights to do as you please, if you wanted to transfer it into dollars or transfer it into Chinese currency or transfer it into lira, whatever. Ownership means you have what is called in Arabic milkiyyah and haqq al-tasarruf: that you have the right to spend as you please. As long as you are the owner, then you may change from one currency to another. And if you think that you're going to make a profit out of it, then it is inherently permissible. There is no sin in it. And again, the issue comes only of full ownership. And that's currency exchange.

Now, as for Forex (and for those of you that don't know, Forex is short for foreign exchange): Forex is not the same as an individual currency transaction between me and you. That's not the same. Forex is a massive multi-trillion-dollar industry.

And Forex trading, I don't want to go into, obviously... And by the way, I've said this many times before: you should realize all people who study Islam have their specialties; they have their strengths and their weaknesses. And as 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said, may Allah have mercy on the one who knows his own weaknesses and deficiencies. And I have no problem publicly stating (I've said this many times) that when it comes to modern Islamic finance, I do not view myself as a specialist and expert. I am a minor student of knowledge who will tell you what the major councils say. If you disagree with what I'm about to say, take it up with those councils. I definitely am qualified to go back and quote you what the councils say and understand what they're saying. I have studied Islamic finance to a level that I'm comfortable where I am, but I personally don't have a desire. Everybody has their desire. I'm much more interested in theology and in aspects of fiqh and in seerah and in history. Everybody is different.

And by the way, you should also know every single scholar is like this. Just like a doctor is not a specialist in all fields of medicine, there is no 'alim in the world that is a global specialist in every single field of the Islamic sciences. It just doesn't exist; it doesn't happen. Just like there's no doctor that is a cutting-edge specialist in every single field of medicine. And so you as the questioner, and also my advice to the students of knowledge and the ulama out there: they as well should humble themselves and know what their own areas are, and inshaAllah, Allah will bless you in this regard.

A famous incident of Imam Malik comes to mind, when somebody came from Andalus with a long series of questions (they say over 30 questions), and for perhaps half, or maybe a third, of them, Imam Malik said, "I don't know this answer; I don't have the answer to this." And this is Imam Malik. So the man said, "O Imam Malik, I have come to you from Andalus, the other side of the world, and I'm going to go back. What do you want me to tell my people, when this is the answer you gave?" And Imam Malik calmly said, "You will go back to your people and you will tell them: Imam Malik said he doesn't know." This is the sign of a real 'alim. May Allah ʿazza wa jall put us in that frame of mind.

So like I said, I never, ever feel myself qualified to go independent in Islamic finance. I am merely a reader and an observer and a quoter; I will quote you what the ulama have said.

So Forex trading is a massive, trillion-dollar industry, and Forex trading is when people buy and sell currencies with the aim to make money on the difference between the two currencies. Now, if it is done individually, as we said, with the previous conditions, it is allowed. But the problem with Forex is that a number of things happen. Of them is that, of course, there's an immense amount of speculation. They're going to buy currency A against currency B in the belief that the price of A will increase against B after some time. And if the currency does increase, then they've made a profit and they're going to close the trade with a gain. However, if the currency decreases in value, the trader will incur a loss. That in and of itself is permissible.

The issue comes that Forex is a platform, and the person who's getting involved is not the sole owner. Rather, they're getting involved with a much larger contract, and you're trading it as an OTC, an over-the-counter transaction. And this means that you speculate on the movement of currencies against each other, but you do not actually take physical ownership of the asset. You do not have milkiyyah; you do not have haqq al-tasarruf. You are only a silent observer: you hand it over, and then if there is a profit you will take it; if there is a loss you will take it. And also there is the added issue of leverage: you are not the sole person. Rather, you will go through a broker, and other people will go through that broker, and you will be lent an imaginary... it's not an imaginary amount, I should say; you will be lent an amount on paper, and then your resources will be pooled together, and then, based upon that, there's going to be a speculative loss or a profit.

And as far as I'm aware, all of the councils that have looked into Forex in detail, all of them have said that Forex is not allowed. And this is the position of the Majma' al-Fiqh al-Islami, which is one of the largest and most respected councils. It is the position of Dar al-Ifta of Egypt. It is the position of the Islamic Council of Malaysia, of Saudi Arabia, of Kuwait. Also Mufti Taqi Usmani, one of the leading contemporary Islamic finance experts, gives a fatwa that it is impermissible.

And if you read the fatawa, it's very clear. There are a number of issues that are brought up, any one of which would invalidate the contract. But a number of them are very clear, in no particular order. Of them, as we said, and I already alluded to this: there is no actual ownership. And our Prophet ﷺ explicitly said, when you're going to buy and sell between these different currencies, it has to be yadan bi-yad. And our Prophet ﷺ said: do not sell what you do not own. And what happens in these Forex markets is that you are essentially buying and selling that which you do not own. You do not have actual ownership in what is being bought or sold, and that is the amount of currency.

Also, another major issue is the issue of leverage. You are getting a loan in return for a profit. You are getting into a dual contract, one of which is a loan, and the other of which is the potential for buying for a profit or a loss based upon that loan. And there is an explicit hadith that you cannot combine a loan with a transaction.

And this is a very important point: one of the fundamental differences between Islamic finance and Western capitalism. Understand this point, whether you like finance or not. By the way, I don't like finance, but anyway, whether you like finance or not... Minds are different. I have never been interested in the financial issues; it's just something that doesn't really concern me that much, alhamdulillah. But anyway, people are different; some people love it. One thing you will definitely understand: in Islam, giving a loan is not a business. It is an act of charity. When you give a loan, you give a loan because you expect Allah to reward you. Our Prophet said that whoever gives a loan for the sake of Allah, Allah will give him 50% of it as a charity. SubhanAllah. If you help your Muslim brother out with a $10,000 loan, you get it back, and guess what? Allah will reward you $5,000 of sadaqah, and you get the money back. SubhanAllah. Can you imagine: you are getting the charity of 50%, and you get to keep the money?

Giving a loan is an act of compassion in Islam. It's an act of charity in Islam. It is not discussed in the book of financial transactions. It's not discussed in the book of profit, the book of businesses, Kitab al-Buyu'. Giving a loan is an act of sadaqah. As for the Western capitalist system, loans are an intrinsic institution in and of themselves to gain a profit. And it is not allowed in our Shari'ah to gain a profit off of a loan. This is a principle in Islamic law, and it is a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ: every single loan that generates a profit, every loan that will guarantee you a profit, it is riba. However you look at it, if you give a loan and you are guaranteed to make a profit, or have a high probability of making a profit, off of that loan (and by high, I mean, like, reasonably, you're going to make one), then you are basically getting into this issue of transforming a loan from an act of worship and sadaqah into a business transaction.

Now, back to our Forex here. In the Forex model, what happens is your amount is leveraged, and on paper you are getting a much larger amount as a loan, but you don't get it; it's not in your pocket anyway. And that loan is then going to be used, leveraged by the amount that you've given, and then, based upon that, the broker, the middleman, the Forex company, is going to speculate and make a massive profit, hopefully, or maybe a loss, whatever the case might be. And so there's the concept of you getting a loan and then using that loan for the sake of speculative profit. So therefore you're combining between the loan and the profit transaction. This is also a very problematic issue, which of course is another reason why our scholars have said Forex is not allowed.

And one of the fatwa councils, the National Fatwa Council of Malaysia, state in their fatwa, and I quote: "A study by the committee found that such trading involves currency speculation, which contradicts Islamic law." This is a point to be added. Allah knows best, it's probably not the strongest point, speculation, but it is there. Because the problem comes: an element of speculation in and of itself does not make something haram. We speculate when it comes to stocks, for example. But anyway, it depends on the level and the quantity and whatnot, and so there is a technical issue there.

The most detailed fatwa that I read in my research was from Dar al-Ifta of Egypt, the official fatwa agency of Egypt. They have, I think, a 10-page fatwa (in Arabic, unfortunately; I don't know anything in English that is in that much detail), in which they did a detailed study, getting the advice of experts, of bankers, of people that are involved in Forex, and so you can see all of the research done there. And they conclude that the general rule is that Forex trading is haram, because of all of these factors and even more, and you can read the online fatwa that is there.

Therefore, to conclude: individual currency exchange is completely halal as long as the two conditions are met. The first condition is that it is done as a spot transaction, and the second condition is that you have the ownership of what you are given. And if it is done, then it is no problem whatsoever, even if it's done for a profit. **However, Forex trading really has many problematic areas, and that is why I am not aware of any fiqh council of the world that has allowed Forex trading.** I ask Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala to bless you with an alternative means to make pure money, and it will be, inshaAllah, better for you.
